**Fontenay-aux-Roses** (French pronunciation:[[fɔ̃tnɛ o ʁoz]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/94/Fr-Paris--Fontenay-aux-Roses.ogg/Fr-Paris--Fontenay-aux-Roses.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fr-Paris--Fontenay-aux-Roses.ogg "File:Fr-Paris--Fontenay-aux-Roses.ogg")) is a [commune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communes_of_France "Communes of France") in the southwestern suburbs of [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), France. It is located 8.6 km (5.3 mi) from the [center of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometre_Zero "Kilometre Zero").

In 1880, a girls' school, the [École normale supérieure de Fontenay-aux-Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_Normale_Sup%C3%A9rieure_de_Fontenay-aux-Roses "École Normale Supérieure de Fontenay-aux-Roses"), was founded with the primary goal of preparing women to become teachers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontenay-aux-Roses#cite_note-3) It became a mixed school in 1986, and was relocated to Lyon in 2000.

Fontenay is the location of the [Commissariat à l'énergie atomique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissariat_%C3%A0_l'%C3%A9nergie_atomique "Commissariat à l'énergie atomique"), and former location of the first French [nuclear reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor "Nuclear reactor"), [Zoé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zo%C3%A9_(reactor) "Zoé (reactor)"), and the first French [tokamak fusion experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokamak "Tokamak"), [TFR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokamak_de_Fontenay_aux_Roses "Tokamak de Fontenay aux Roses").

## Name

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fontenay-aux-Roses&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Name")]

The commune name originates from a local spring-fed stream (Latin _fons_, French _fontaine_) in the hillside descending from the Châtillon plateau, with "of roses" added to distinguish this commune from numerous French communes named Fontenay.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fontenay-aux-Roses&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

The [Hôtel de Ville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville,_Fontenay-aux-Roses "Hôtel de Ville, Fontenay-aux-Roses") was completed in 1860.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontenay-aux-Roses#cite_note-4)

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fontenay-aux-Roses&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Climate")]

The climate of Fontenay-aux-Roses is oceanic gradient. The observation stations used for the weather in Fontenay are at Orly and the airport of [Velizy-Villacoublay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A9lizy_%E2%80%93_Villacoublay_Air_Base "Vélizy – Villacoublay Air Base"), municipalities located not far from Fontenay. The climate is characterised by sunshine and fairly low rainfall. The average rainfall is about 650 mm per year, spread over 111 rainy days on average, including 16 days of heavy rainfall (10 mm). Temperatures are mild; the coldest month is January with an average temperature of 4.7°C and the hottest months are July and August with a mean temperature of 20°C.

Severe weather conditions are sometimes recorded:

*   Maximum Temperature: 42.0°C in 2003;
*   Minimum Temperature: -16.0°C in 1985;
*   Maximum rain in 24 hours: 100 mm from 6 p.m. on 30th to 6 p.m. on August 5, 1997;
*   High temperature days (> 25°C): 59.3;
*   Rain days: 120.

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fontenay-aux-Roses&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Education")]

Primary schools in the commune:[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontenay-aux-Roses#cite_note-8)

*   Six public preschools (_maternelles_): La Roue, Les Ormeaux, Les Pervenches, Les Renards, Jean Macé, Scarron
*   Six public elementary schools: La Roue A, La Roue B, Le Parc, Les Ormeaux, Les Pervenches, Les Renards
*   One private preschool and elementary school: Maternelle et Élémentaire St-Vincent de Paul

There is a public junior high school, Collège les Ormeaux.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontenay-aux-Roses#cite_note-9)

[Lycée professionnel privé Saint François d'Assise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_professionnel_priv%C3%A9_Saint_Fran%C3%A7ois_d'Assise?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lycée professionnel privé Saint François d'Assise (page does not exist)"), a private vocational high school, is in the commune.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontenay-aux-Roses#cite_note-10)

**Fontenay-aux-Roses** (French pronunciation:[[fɔ̃tnɛ o ʁoz]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/94/Fr-Paris--Fontenay-aux-Roses.ogg/Fr-Paris--Fontenay-aux-Roses.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fr-Paris--Fontenay-aux-Roses.ogg "File:Fr-Paris--Fontenay-aux-Roses.ogg")) is a [commune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communes_of_France "Communes of France") in the southwestern suburbs of [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), France. It is located 8.6 km (5.3 mi) from the [center of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometre_Zero "Kilometre Zero").

In 1880, a girls' school, the [École normale supérieure de Fontenay-aux-Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_Normale_Sup%C3%A9rieure_de_Fontenay-aux-Roses "École Normale Supérieure de Fontenay-aux-Roses"), was founded with the primary goal of preparing women to become teachers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontenay-aux-Roses#cite_note-3) It became a mixed school in 1986, and was relocated to Lyon in 2000.

Fontenay is the location of the [Commissariat à l'énergie atomique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissariat_%C3%A0_l'%C3%A9nergie_atomique "Commissariat à l'énergie atomique"), and former location of the first French [nuclear reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor "Nuclear reactor"), [Zoé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zo%C3%A9_(reactor) "Zoé (reactor)"), and the first French [tokamak fusion experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokamak "Tokamak"), [TFR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokamak_de_Fontenay_aux_Roses "Tokamak de Fontenay aux Roses").

## Name

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fontenay-aux-Roses&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Name")]

The commune name originates from a local spring-fed stream (Latin _fons_, French _fontaine_) in the hillside descending from the Châtillon plateau, with "of roses" added to distinguish this commune from numerous French communes named Fontenay.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fontenay-aux-Roses&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

The [Hôtel de Ville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville,_Fontenay-aux-Roses "Hôtel de Ville, Fontenay-aux-Roses") was completed in 1860.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontenay-aux-Roses#cite_note-4)

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fontenay-aux-Roses&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Climate")]

The climate of Fontenay-aux-Roses is oceanic gradient. The observation stations used for the weather in Fontenay are at Orly and the airport of [Velizy-Villacoublay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A9lizy_%E2%80%93_Villacoublay_Air_Base "Vélizy – Villacoublay Air Base"), municipalities located not far from Fontenay. The climate is characterised by sunshine and fairly low rainfall. The average rainfall is about 650 mm per year, spread over 111 rainy days on average, including 16 days of heavy rainfall (10 mm). Temperatures are mild; the coldest month is January with an average temperature of 4.7°C and the hottest months are July and August with a mean temperature of 20°C.

Severe weather conditions are sometimes recorded:

*   Maximum Temperature: 42.0°C in 2003;
*   Minimum Temperature: -16.0°C in 1985;
*   Maximum rain in 24 hours: 100 mm from 6 p.m. on 30th to 6 p.m. on August 5, 1997;
*   High temperature days (> 25°C): 59.3;
*   Rain days: 120.

## Personalities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fontenay-aux-Roses&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personalities")]

*   [Paul Scarron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Scarron "Paul Scarron") (1610–1660) – writer, lived in Fontenay-aux-Roses.
*   [Theresa Cabarrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9r%C3%A9sa_Tallien "Thérésa Tallien") (1773–1835) – Known as "Madame Tallien" whose residence has become the École Normale Supérieure de Fontenay-aux-Roses.
*   [Aristide Boucicaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristide_Boucicaut "Aristide Boucicaut") (1810–1877) – Founder of the Bon Marché and benefactor of the town, has long lived in Fontenay where he owned a large residence (known as the "castle Boucicaut and razed in 1954) it was also a member of the municipal council and was even elected mayor in 1871. However, he refused the post, and preferred to remain an alderman.
*   [Joris-Karl Huysmans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joris-Karl_Huysmans "Joris-Karl Huysmans") (1848–1907) – Worked in Fontenay in July 1881 on his novel _À Rebours_; it is the setting for the aesthetic experiments of the decadent aristocrat des Esseintes.
*   [Ferdinand Lot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Lot "Ferdinand Lot") (1866–1952) – medieval historian, lived in Fontenay-aux-Roses for a long time; he is buried in the family tomb.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Technique of painting with small, distinct dots

Main article: [Neo-Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Impressionism "Neo-Impressionism")

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Seurat-La_Parade_detail.jpg/250px-Seurat-La_Parade_detail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seurat-La_Parade_detail.jpg)

Detail from [Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat")'s _[Parade de cirque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parade\_de\_cirque "Parade de cirque")_, 1889, showing the contrasting dots of paint which define Pointillism

**Pointillism** ([/ˈ p w æ̃t ɪ l ɪ z əm/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"), also [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English "American English"): [/ˈ p w ɑː n-ˌ ˈ p ɔɪ n-/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"))[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-1) is a technique of [painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painting "Painting") in which small, distinct dots of color are applied in patterns to form an image.

[Georges Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat") and [Paul Signac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac "Paul Signac") developed the technique in 1886, branching from [Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism"). The term "Pointillism" was coined by [art critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_critics "Art critics") in the late 1880s to ridicule the works of these artists, but is now used without its earlier pejorative connotation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-ArtCyclopedia-2) The movement Seurat began with this technique is known as [Neo-impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-impressionism "Neo-impressionism"). The [Divisionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisionism "Divisionism") used a similar technique of patterns to form images, though with larger cube-like brushstrokes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-3)

## Technique

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pointillism&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Technique")]

The technique relies on the ability of the eye and mind of the viewer to blend the color spots into a fuller range of tones. It is related to [Divisionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisionism "Divisionism"), a more technical variant of the method. Divisionism is concerned with [color theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_theory "Color theory"), whereas pointillism is more focused on the specific style of brushwork used to apply the paint.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-ArtCyclopedia-2) Pointillism is a technique with few serious practitioners today and is notably seen in the works of [Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat"), [Signac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac "Paul Signac"), and [Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Edmond_Cross "Henri-Edmond Cross").

From 1905 to 1907, [Robert Delaunay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Delaunay "Robert Delaunay") and [Jean Metzinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Metzinger "Jean Metzinger") painted in a Divisionist style with large squares or 'cubes' of color: the size and direction of each gave a sense of rhythm to the painting, yet color varied independently of size and placement.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Jean_Metzinger-4) This form of Divisionism was a significant step beyond the preoccupations of Signac and Cross. In 1906, the art critic Louis Chassevent recognized the difference and, as art historian [Daniel Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Robbins_(art_historian) "Daniel Robbins (art historian)") pointed out, used the word "cube" which would later be taken up by [Louis Vauxcelles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Vauxcelles "Louis Vauxcelles") to baptize [Cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism"). Chassevent writes:

M. Metzinger is a mosaicist like M. Signac but he brings more precision to the cutting of his cubes of color which appear to have been made mechanically [...].[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Daniel_Robbins-8)

## Practice

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pointillism&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Practice")]

The practice of Pointillism is in sharp contrast to the traditional methods of blending pigments on a [palette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palette_(painting) "Palette (painting)"). Pointillism is analogous to the four-color [CMYK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMYK_color_model "CMYK color model") printing process used by some color printers and large presses that place dots of [cyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyan "Cyan"), [magenta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magenta "Magenta"), yellow, and key (black). Televisions and computer monitors use a similar technique to represent image colors using [red, green and blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RGB_color_model "RGB color model") (RGB) colors.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Greene-9)

If red, blue, and green light (the [additive primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_color#handprintprimaries "Primary color")) are mixed, the result is something close to white light (see [Prism (optics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prism_(optics) "Prism (optics)")). Painting is inherently [subtractive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_color#handprintprimaries "Primary color"), but Pointillist colors often seem brighter than typical mixed subtractive colors. This may be partly because subtractive mixing of the pigments is avoided, and because some of the white canvas may be showing between the applied dots.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Greene-9)

The painting technique used for Pointillist color mixing is at the expense of the traditional brushwork used to delineate [texture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_(visual_arts) "Texture (visual arts)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Greene-9)

The majority of Pointillism is done in oil paint. Anything may be used in its place, but oils are preferred for their thickness and tendency not to run or bleed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-10)

## Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pointillism&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Music")]

Pointillism also refers to a style of 20th-century music composition. Different musical notes are made in seclusion, rather than in a linear sequence, giving a sound texture similar to the painting version of Pointillism. This type of music is also known as [punctualism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punctualism "Punctualism") or [klangfarbenmelodie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klangfarbenmelodie "Klangfarbenmelodie").

In the 21st century, Australian composer [Georges Lentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Lentz "Georges Lentz")’s music, influenced by the subtle dot paintings of [Kathleen Petyarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathleen_Petyarre "Kathleen Petyarre") and by the starry night sky in the Australian Outback, has also, in some aspects, been described as pointillistic.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-11)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Technique of painting with small, distinct dots

Main article: [Neo-Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Impressionism "Neo-Impressionism")

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Seurat-La_Parade_detail.jpg/250px-Seurat-La_Parade_detail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seurat-La_Parade_detail.jpg)

Detail from [Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat")'s _[Parade de cirque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parade\_de\_cirque "Parade de cirque")_, 1889, showing the contrasting dots of paint which define Pointillism

**Pointillism** ([/ˈ p w æ̃t ɪ l ɪ z əm/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"), also [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English "American English"): [/ˈ p w ɑː n-ˌ ˈ p ɔɪ n-/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"))[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-1) is a technique of [painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painting "Painting") in which small, distinct dots of color are applied in patterns to form an image.

[Georges Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat") and [Paul Signac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac "Paul Signac") developed the technique in 1886, branching from [Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism"). The term "Pointillism" was coined by [art critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_critics "Art critics") in the late 1880s to ridicule the works of these artists, but is now used without its earlier pejorative connotation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-ArtCyclopedia-2) The movement Seurat began with this technique is known as [Neo-impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-impressionism "Neo-impressionism"). The [Divisionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisionism "Divisionism") used a similar technique of patterns to form images, though with larger cube-like brushstrokes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-3)

## Technique

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pointillism&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Technique")]

The technique relies on the ability of the eye and mind of the viewer to blend the color spots into a fuller range of tones. It is related to [Divisionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisionism "Divisionism"), a more technical variant of the method. Divisionism is concerned with [color theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_theory "Color theory"), whereas pointillism is more focused on the specific style of brushwork used to apply the paint.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-ArtCyclopedia-2) Pointillism is a technique with few serious practitioners today and is notably seen in the works of [Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat"), [Signac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac "Paul Signac"), and [Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Edmond_Cross "Henri-Edmond Cross").

From 1905 to 1907, [Robert Delaunay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Delaunay "Robert Delaunay") and [Jean Metzinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Metzinger "Jean Metzinger") painted in a Divisionist style with large squares or 'cubes' of color: the size and direction of each gave a sense of rhythm to the painting, yet color varied independently of size and placement.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Jean_Metzinger-4) This form of Divisionism was a significant step beyond the preoccupations of Signac and Cross. In 1906, the art critic Louis Chassevent recognized the difference and, as art historian [Daniel Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Robbins_(art_historian) "Daniel Robbins (art historian)") pointed out, used the word "cube" which would later be taken up by [Louis Vauxcelles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Vauxcelles "Louis Vauxcelles") to baptize [Cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism"). Chassevent writes:

M. Metzinger is a mosaicist like M. Signac but he brings more precision to the cutting of his cubes of color which appear to have been made mechanically [...].[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Daniel_Robbins-8)

## Practice

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pointillism&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Practice")]

The practice of Pointillism is in sharp contrast to the traditional methods of blending pigments on a [palette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palette_(painting) "Palette (painting)"). Pointillism is analogous to the four-color [CMYK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMYK_color_model "CMYK color model") printing process used by some color printers and large presses that place dots of [cyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyan "Cyan"), [magenta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magenta "Magenta"), yellow, and key (black). Televisions and computer monitors use a similar technique to represent image colors using [red, green and blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RGB_color_model "RGB color model") (RGB) colors.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Greene-9)

If red, blue, and green light (the [additive primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_color#handprintprimaries "Primary color")) are mixed, the result is something close to white light (see [Prism (optics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prism_(optics) "Prism (optics)")). Painting is inherently [subtractive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_color#handprintprimaries "Primary color"), but Pointillist colors often seem brighter than typical mixed subtractive colors. This may be partly because subtractive mixing of the pigments is avoided, and because some of the white canvas may be showing between the applied dots.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Greene-9)

The painting technique used for Pointillist color mixing is at the expense of the traditional brushwork used to delineate [texture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_(visual_arts) "Texture (visual arts)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-Greene-9)

The majority of Pointillism is done in oil paint. Anything may be used in its place, but oils are preferred for their thickness and tendency not to run or bleed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-10)

## Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pointillism&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Music")]

Pointillism also refers to a style of 20th-century music composition. Different musical notes are made in seclusion, rather than in a linear sequence, giving a sound texture similar to the painting version of Pointillism. This type of music is also known as [punctualism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punctualism "Punctualism") or [klangfarbenmelodie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klangfarbenmelodie "Klangfarbenmelodie").

In the 21st century, Australian composer [Georges Lentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Lentz "Georges Lentz")’s music, influenced by the subtle dot paintings of [Kathleen Petyarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathleen_Petyarre "Kathleen Petyarre") and by the starry night sky in the Australian Outback, has also, in some aspects, been described as pointillistic.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism#cite_note-11)

The meeting began on the same day that an American actor, known for their role in the television series Lou Grant, passed away. Later, an exhibition at a university gallery featured over 10 original artworks from the project, including woodcut prints by Person 4.
