In 1886 Signac met [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh") in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"). During 1887 the two artists regularly went to [Asnières-sur-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asni%C3%A8res-sur-Seine "Asnières-sur-Seine") together, where they painted such subjects as river landscapes and cafés. Initially, Van Gogh chiefly admired Signac's loose painting technique. Signac also met [Toulouse Lautrec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec "Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec"), who was a friend of Van Gogh.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-8)

In March 1889, Signac visited Van Gogh at [Arles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arles "Arles"). In 1890, during the banquet of the [XX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_XX "Les XX") exhibition in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), Lautrec challenged to a duel the artist [Henri de Groux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_de_Groux "Henry de Groux") who criticized Van Gogh's works. Signac declared he would continue to fight for Van Gogh’s honor if Lautrec was killed. De Groux apologized for the slight and left the group and the duel never took place.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-9)

The next year he made a short trip to Italy, seeing [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), and [Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naples "Naples").

In 1888, Signac discovered [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchist "Anarchist") ideas by reading [Élisée Reclus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89lis%C3%A9e_Reclus "Élisée Reclus"), [Kropotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kropotkin "Kropotkin"), and [Jean Grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Grave "Jean Grave"), who all developed the ideas of anarchist communism. With his friends Charles Angrand, Henri-Edmond Cross, [Maximilien Luce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilien_Luce "Maximilien Luce"), and [Camille Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Pissarro "Camille Pissarro") he contributed to Jean Grave's paper, _Les Temps Nouveaux_ (New Times).

In 1892, he sailed the [Garonne River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garonne_River "Garonne River") southeast in France to the Mediterranean Sea, spending time in Saint-Tropez.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerretti-Bocquillon2001304-10)

Signac experimented with various media. As well as oil paintings and [watercolors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watercolor_painting "Watercolor painting") he made [etchings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etching "Etching"), [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography"), and many pen-and-ink sketches composed of small, laborious dots.

The Neo-Impressionists influenced the next generation: Signac inspired [Henri Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Matisse "Henri Matisse"), [André Derain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Derain "André Derain") and his friend [Robert Deborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Deborne "Robert Deborne") in particular, thus playing a decisive role in the evolution of [Fauvism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauvism "Fauvism"). Signac himself did not admire the style when it first appeared.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-11)

Having prospered well, his financial support of the arts was considerable. As donations, he sent regular cheques and made a gift of his works for five lotteries between 1895 and 1912.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-PaulSignac-12) Signac's 1893 painting, _In the Time of Harmony_ originally was entitled, _In the Time of Anarchy_, but political repression targeting the anarchists in France at this time forced him to change the title before the work could be accepted by a gallery.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-Alex_Butterworth-13)

At the 1905 Salon des Indépendants, [Henri Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Matisse "Henri Matisse") exhibited the proto-[Fauve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauvism "Fauvism") painting _[Luxe, Calme et Volupté](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxe,\_Calme\_et\_Volupt%C3%A9 "Luxe, Calme et Volupté")_. The brightly colored composition was painted in 1904 after a summer spent working in [St. Tropez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Tropez "St. Tropez") on the [French Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Riviera "French Riviera") alongside the [neo-Impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Impressionism "Neo-Impressionism") painters [Henri-Edmond Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Edmond_Cross "Henri-Edmond Cross") and Paul Signac.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-14) The painting is Matisse's most important work in which he used the [Divisionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisionism "Divisionism") technique advocated by Signac, which Matisse had adopted in 1898 after reading Signac's essay, _d'Eugène Delacroix au Néo-Impressionnisme_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-16) Signac purchased the work after the 1905 Salon des Indépendants. In 1908 Signac was elected president of the Twenty-fourth Salon des Indépendants.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-Clement-17)

As president of the [Société des Artistes Indépendants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9_des_Artistes_Ind%C3%A9pendants "Société des Artistes Indépendants"), from 1908 until his death, Signac encouraged younger artists by exhibiting the controversial works of the Fauves and the [Cubists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism"). He was the first patron to buy a painting by Matisse.

Signac served as a juror with [Florence Meyer Blumenthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Meyer_Blumenthal "Florence Meyer Blumenthal") in awarding the _[Prix Blumenthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prix\_Blumenthal "Prix Blumenthal")_, a grant given between 1919 and 1954 to painters, sculptors, decorators, engravers, writers, and musicians.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-FMBlumenthal-18)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Signac&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Personal life")]

On 7 November 1892, Signac married Berthe Roblès at the town hall of the [18th arrondissement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_arrondissement_of_Paris "18th arrondissement of Paris"). The witnesses at the wedding were Alexandre Lemonier, [Maximilien Luce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilien_Luce "Maximilien Luce"), [Camille Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Pissarro "Camille Pissarro"), and [Georges Lecomte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Lecomte "Georges Lecomte").

In November 1897, the Signacs moved to a new apartment in the _[Castel Béranger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castel\_B%C3%A9ranger "Castel Béranger")_, which was built by [Hector Guimard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hector_Guimard "Hector Guimard"). A little later, in December of the same year, they acquired a house in [Saint-Tropez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Tropez "Saint-Tropez") named _La Hune_ where the painter had a vast studio constructed that he inaugurated on 16 August 1898.

In September 1913, Signac rented a house at [Antibes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibes "Antibes"), where he took up residence with [Jeanne Selmersheim-Desgrange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Selmersheim-Desgrange "Jeanne Selmersheim-Desgrange"). She gave birth to their daughter, Ginette, on 2 October 1913. Meanwhile, Signac left _La Hune_ and the _Castel Beranger_ apartment to Berthe and they remained friends for the rest of his life. On 6 April 1927, Signac formally adopted Ginette. His granddaughter, [Françoise Cachin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7oise_Cachin "Françoise Cachin"), was an art historian.

Paul Signac died from [sepsis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sepsis "Sepsis") in Paris on 15 August 1935 at the age of 71. His body was cremated and was interred three days later, on 18 August, at the [Père Lachaise Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A8re_Lachaise_Cemetery "Père Lachaise Cemetery").

## Author

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Signac&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Author")]

Signac wrote several important works on the theory of art, among them, _From Eugène Delacroix to Neo-Impressionism_, first published in serial form in 1898. It is an important history of color and explanation of neo-impressionist technique. It also discusses [Johan Barthold Jongkind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Barthold_Jongkind "Johan Barthold Jongkind") (1819–1891). Signac also authored several introductions to the catalogues of art exhibitions and many other writings yet to be published.

Politically, he was an [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchist "Anarchist"), as were many of his friends, including [Félix Fénéon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9lix_F%C3%A9n%C3%A9on "Félix Fénéon"), [Maximilien Luce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilien_Luce "Maximilien Luce") and [Camille Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Pissarro "Camille Pissarro").

**Paul Victor Jules Signac** ([/s iː n ˈ j ɑː k/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_seen-YAHK_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-1)French:[[pɔl siɲak]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French"); 11 November 1863 – 15 August 1935) was a French [Neo-Impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-impressionism "Neo-impressionism")[painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painting "Painting") who, with [Georges Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat"), helped develop the artistic technique Pointillism.

A keen sailor, he is best known for his seascapes and views of ports and rivers.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Signac&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Paul-Victor-Jules Signac was born in Paris on 11 November 1863.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerretti-Bocquillon2001297-2) His parents wanted him to study [architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture "Architecture") but, as he said, his preference was to draw [the Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Seine "The Seine"). He was particularly affected by an 1880 exhibition of [Claude Monet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Monet "Claude Monet")'s work. Signac began boating.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerretti-Bocquillon2001298-3)

[![Image 7: painting](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Paul_Signac%2C_1893%2C_Femme_%C3%A0_l%27ombrelle%2C_oil_on_canvas%2C_81_x_65_cm%2C_Mus%C3%A9e_d%27Orsay.jpg/250px-Paul_Signac%2C_1893%2C_Femme_%C3%A0_l%27ombrelle%2C_oil_on_canvas%2C_81_x_65_cm%2C_Mus%C3%A9e_d%27Orsay.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_Signac,_1893,_Femme_%C3%A0_l'ombrelle,_oil_on_canvas,_81_x_65_cm,_Mus%C3%A9e_d'Orsay.jpg)

In 1884 he met [Claude Monet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Monet "Claude Monet") and [Georges Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat"). He was struck by the systematic working methods of Seurat and by his theory of colors and he became Seurat's faithful supporter, friend, and heir with his description of [Neo-Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Impressionism "Neo-Impressionism") and [Divisionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisionism "Divisionism") method.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-4) Under Seurat's influence he abandoned the short brushstrokes of [Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism") to experiment with scientifically-juxtaposed small dots of pure color, intended to combine and blend not on the canvas, but in the viewer's eye, the defining feature of Pointillism.

The Mediterranean coast is a major theme across Signac's paintings.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-5) He left the capital each summer, to stay in the south of France in the village of Collioure or at [St. Tropez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Tropez "St. Tropez"), where he bought a house and invited his friends. He envisioned the south of France as the perfect location for a future anarchist utopia.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-6)

Signac, [Albert Dubois-Pillet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Dubois-Pillet "Albert Dubois-Pillet"), [Odilon Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odilon_Redon "Odilon Redon"), and Seurat were among the founders of the [Société des Artistes Indépendants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9_des_Artistes_Ind%C3%A9pendants "Société des Artistes Indépendants"). The association began in Paris 29 July 1884 with the organization of massive exhibitions, embracing as their motto, "Neither jury nor awards" (_Sans jury ni récompense_). "The purpose of Société des Artistes Indépendants—based on the principle of abolishing admission jury—is to allow the artists to present their works to public judgement with complete freedom".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-Ind%C3%A9pendants-7) For the following three decades their annual exhibitions flourished and set the trends in art of the early twentieth century. Signac was a guiding force in the Société and was its President from 1908 until his death.

In 1886 Signac met [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh") in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"). During 1887 the two artists regularly went to [Asnières-sur-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asni%C3%A8res-sur-Seine "Asnières-sur-Seine") together, where they painted such subjects as river landscapes and cafés. Initially, Van Gogh chiefly admired Signac's loose painting technique. Signac also met [Toulouse Lautrec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec "Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec"), who was a friend of Van Gogh.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-8)

In March 1889, Signac visited Van Gogh at [Arles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arles "Arles"). In 1890, during the banquet of the [XX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_XX "Les XX") exhibition in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), Lautrec challenged to a duel the artist [Henri de Groux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_de_Groux "Henry de Groux") who criticized Van Gogh's works. Signac declared he would continue to fight for Van Gogh’s honor if Lautrec was killed. De Groux apologized for the slight and left the group and the duel never took place.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-9)

The next year he made a short trip to Italy, seeing [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), and [Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naples "Naples").

In 1888, Signac discovered [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchist "Anarchist") ideas by reading [Élisée Reclus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89lis%C3%A9e_Reclus "Élisée Reclus"), [Kropotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kropotkin "Kropotkin"), and [Jean Grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Grave "Jean Grave"), who all developed the ideas of anarchist communism. With his friends Charles Angrand, Henri-Edmond Cross, [Maximilien Luce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilien_Luce "Maximilien Luce"), and [Camille Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Pissarro "Camille Pissarro") he contributed to Jean Grave's paper, _Les Temps Nouveaux_ (New Times).

In 1892, he sailed the [Garonne River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garonne_River "Garonne River") southeast in France to the Mediterranean Sea, spending time in Saint-Tropez.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerretti-Bocquillon2001304-10)

Signac experimented with various media. As well as oil paintings and [watercolors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watercolor_painting "Watercolor painting") he made [etchings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etching "Etching"), [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography"), and many pen-and-ink sketches composed of small, laborious dots.

The Neo-Impressionists influenced the next generation: Signac inspired [Henri Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Matisse "Henri Matisse"), [André Derain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Derain "André Derain") and his friend [Robert Deborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Deborne "Robert Deborne") in particular, thus playing a decisive role in the evolution of [Fauvism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauvism "Fauvism"). Signac himself did not admire the style when it first appeared.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-11)

Having prospered well, his financial support of the arts was considerable. As donations, he sent regular cheques and made a gift of his works for five lotteries between 1895 and 1912.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-PaulSignac-12) Signac's 1893 painting, _In the Time of Harmony_ originally was entitled, _In the Time of Anarchy_, but political repression targeting the anarchists in France at this time forced him to change the title before the work could be accepted by a gallery.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-Alex_Butterworth-13)

At the 1905 Salon des Indépendants, [Henri Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Matisse "Henri Matisse") exhibited the proto-[Fauve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauvism "Fauvism") painting _[Luxe, Calme et Volupté](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxe,\_Calme\_et\_Volupt%C3%A9 "Luxe, Calme et Volupté")_. The brightly colored composition was painted in 1904 after a summer spent working in [St. Tropez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Tropez "St. Tropez") on the [French Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Riviera "French Riviera") alongside the [neo-Impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Impressionism "Neo-Impressionism") painters [Henri-Edmond Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Edmond_Cross "Henri-Edmond Cross") and Paul Signac.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-14) The painting is Matisse's most important work in which he used the [Divisionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisionism "Divisionism") technique advocated by Signac, which Matisse had adopted in 1898 after reading Signac's essay, _d'Eugène Delacroix au Néo-Impressionnisme_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-16) Signac purchased the work after the 1905 Salon des Indépendants. In 1908 Signac was elected president of the Twenty-fourth Salon des Indépendants.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-Clement-17)

As president of the [Société des Artistes Indépendants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9_des_Artistes_Ind%C3%A9pendants "Société des Artistes Indépendants"), from 1908 until his death, Signac encouraged younger artists by exhibiting the controversial works of the Fauves and the [Cubists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism"). He was the first patron to buy a painting by Matisse.

Signac served as a juror with [Florence Meyer Blumenthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Meyer_Blumenthal "Florence Meyer Blumenthal") in awarding the _[Prix Blumenthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prix\_Blumenthal "Prix Blumenthal")_, a grant given between 1919 and 1954 to painters, sculptors, decorators, engravers, writers, and musicians.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac#cite_note-FMBlumenthal-18)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Signac&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Personal life")]

On 7 November 1892, Signac married Berthe Roblès at the town hall of the [18th arrondissement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_arrondissement_of_Paris "18th arrondissement of Paris"). The witnesses at the wedding were Alexandre Lemonier, [Maximilien Luce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilien_Luce "Maximilien Luce"), [Camille Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Pissarro "Camille Pissarro"), and [Georges Lecomte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Lecomte "Georges Lecomte").

In November 1897, the Signacs moved to a new apartment in the _[Castel Béranger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castel\_B%C3%A9ranger "Castel Béranger")_, which was built by [Hector Guimard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hector_Guimard "Hector Guimard"). A little later, in December of the same year, they acquired a house in [Saint-Tropez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Tropez "Saint-Tropez") named _La Hune_ where the painter had a vast studio constructed that he inaugurated on 16 August 1898.

In September 1913, Signac rented a house at [Antibes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibes "Antibes"), where he took up residence with [Jeanne Selmersheim-Desgrange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Selmersheim-Desgrange "Jeanne Selmersheim-Desgrange"). She gave birth to their daughter, Ginette, on 2 October 1913. Meanwhile, Signac left _La Hune_ and the _Castel Beranger_ apartment to Berthe and they remained friends for the rest of his life. On 6 April 1927, Signac formally adopted Ginette. His granddaughter, [Françoise Cachin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7oise_Cachin "Françoise Cachin"), was an art historian.

Paul Signac died from [sepsis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sepsis "Sepsis") in Paris on 15 August 1935 at the age of 71. His body was cremated and was interred three days later, on 18 August, at the [Père Lachaise Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A8re_Lachaise_Cemetery "Père Lachaise Cemetery").

## Author

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Signac&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Author")]

Signac wrote several important works on the theory of art, among them, _From Eugène Delacroix to Neo-Impressionism_, first published in serial form in 1898. It is an important history of color and explanation of neo-impressionist technique. It also discusses [Johan Barthold Jongkind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Barthold_Jongkind "Johan Barthold Jongkind") (1819–1891). Signac also authored several introductions to the catalogues of art exhibitions and many other writings yet to be published.

Politically, he was an [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchist "Anarchist"), as were many of his friends, including [Félix Fénéon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9lix_F%C3%A9n%C3%A9on "Félix Fénéon"), [Maximilien Luce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilien_Luce "Maximilien Luce") and [Camille Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Pissarro "Camille Pissarro").

The **Association for Art History** (**AAH**) (formerly **Association of Art Historians**) is a British organisation promoting the professional practice and public understanding of [art history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_history "Art history"). Formed in 1974 as the **Association of Art Historians**,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-1) it rebranded in 2016.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-old-2) It is based in London and is a [registered charity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registered_charity "Registered charity") (No. 1154066).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-cc-3)

## Membership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Membership")]

Individual membership is open to anyone with a professional commitment to and interest in art history and visual culture. Institutional membership is also available.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-4)

## Governance and financial

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Governance and financial")]

The Association is governed by a board of trustees. For the year ended 31 December 2010, the AAH had a gross income of £396,818 and expenditure of £359,507 according to accounts filed with the [Charity Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charity_Commission "Charity Commission").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-cc-3)

## Publications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Publications")]

There is a quarterly newsletter, the _Bulletin_, and a peer-reviewed scholarly journal _[Art History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art\_History\_(journal) "Art History (journal)")_ published five times a year in association with [Wiley-Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiley-Blackwell "Wiley-Blackwell").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-5)

## Events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Events")]

Events include an annual conference, held in April.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-8)

## Affiliations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Affiliations")]

The AAH is affiliated with the US [College Art Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Art_Association "College Art Association") (CAA) and supports the [Comité International d'Histoire de l'Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comit%C3%A9_International_d'Histoire_de_l'Art "Comité International d'Histoire de l'Art") (CIHA).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-old-2)

The **Association for Art History** (**AAH**) (formerly **Association of Art Historians**) is a British organisation promoting the professional practice and public understanding of [art history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_history "Art history"). Formed in 1974 as the **Association of Art Historians**,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-1) it rebranded in 2016.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-old-2) It is based in London and is a [registered charity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registered_charity "Registered charity") (No. 1154066).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-cc-3)

## Membership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Membership")]

Individual membership is open to anyone with a professional commitment to and interest in art history and visual culture. Institutional membership is also available.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-4)

## Governance and financial

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Governance and financial")]

The Association is governed by a board of trustees. For the year ended 31 December 2010, the AAH had a gross income of £396,818 and expenditure of £359,507 according to accounts filed with the [Charity Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charity_Commission "Charity Commission").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-cc-3)

## Publications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Publications")]

There is a quarterly newsletter, the _Bulletin_, and a peer-reviewed scholarly journal _[Art History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art\_History\_(journal) "Art History (journal)")_ published five times a year in association with [Wiley-Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiley-Blackwell "Wiley-Blackwell").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-5)

## Events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Events")]

Events include an annual conference, held in April.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-8)

## Affiliations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_Art_History&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Affiliations")]

The AAH is affiliated with the US [College Art Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Art_Association "College Art Association") (CAA) and supports the [Comité International d'Histoire de l'Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comit%C3%A9_International_d'Histoire_de_l'Art "Comité International d'Histoire de l'Art") (CIHA).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Art_Historians#cite_note-old-2)

# ANNUAL CONFERENCE

The annual event for art history in the UK.

Our Annual Conference brings together international research and critical debate about art, art history and visual cultures. This key annual event is an opportunity to keep up to date with new research, hear leading keynotes, broaden networks and exchange ideas.

The Annual Conference is open to all. It is a key annual event for those presenting new research, and those wanting to listen and learn about new research. Attracting around 500 attendees each year, the conference is popular with academics, curators, practitioners, Phd students, early career researchers and non-art historians engaged with art history research. # 2024 Annual Conference

**3-5 April 2024**

**University of Bristol**

[**Booking now open!**](https://www.eventbrite.co.uk/e/association-for-art-history-annual-conference-2024-tickets-759699360237?aff=oddtdtcreator)

**2024 marks the fiftieth anniversary of the Association for Art History**. We are delighted to announce that our 50 th annual conference will be held in collaboration with the History of Art department at the**University of Bristol**.

The Association for Art History’s Annual Conference brings together international research and critical debate about art history and visual culture. A key annual event, the conference is an opportunity to keep up to date with new research, hear leading keynotes, broaden networks and exchange ideas.

The 2024 Annual Conference is open to all, members and non-members of the Association for Art History. Members of the Association get reduced conference rates, and concessionary tickets are also available.

Details on each session can be found below, and the [Programme at a Glance](https://forarthistory.org.uk/conference/2024-annual-conference/2024-programme-at-a-glance-2/) page provides information on the entire schedule.

Conference tickets are now available and include access to all sessions, keynotes, exhibitors, visits, professional programme events and networking opportunities.

Further information about tickets can be found on the booking page –[**BOOK NOW**](https://www.eventbrite.co.uk/e/association-for-art-history-annual-conference-2024-tickets-759699360237?aff=oddtdtcreator)

**Wednesday 3 April: Re-thinking Black Art: curatorial models**

*   **Paul Goodwin, University of the Arts, London**

*   **AAH Chair, Christopher Breward, Director of National Museums Scotland joins former AAH Chairs Christine Riding, The National Gallery, London, Evelyn Welch, University of Bristol and Nigel Llewellyn, Independent, for a conversation with our CEO Gregory Perry**

**2024 marks the fiftieth anniversary of the Association for Art History**. We are delighted to announce that our 50 th annual conference will be held in collaboration with the History of Art department at the**University of Bristol**.

The Association for Art History’s Annual Conference brings together international research and critical debate about art history and visual culture. A key annual event, the conference is an opportunity to keep up to date with new research, hear leading keynotes, broaden networks and exchange ideas.

The 2024 Annual Conference is open to all, members and non-members of the Association for Art History. Members of the Association get reduced conference rates, and concessionary tickets are also available.

# 2023 Annual Conference

**12-14 APRIL 2023**  
**University College London**

**Welcome!**

We are delighted to welcome you to our **49 th Annual Conference** taking place in-person over three engaging days at **University College London**.

**#ForArtHistory2023** is an opportunity to keep up to date with new research, hear leading keynotes, broaden networks and exchange ideas. Foregrounding critical debate about art, art history and visual cultures in a supportive and inclusive environment is a key remit of the event ensuring that panels and contributing papers represent diverse approaches to the discipline.

Our Annual Conference is open to all and will appeal to academics, curators, practitioners, PhD students, early career researchers and non-art historians engaged with art history research. Members of the Association get reduced conference rates, and concessionary tickets are also available.

Details on each session can be found below.

Conference tickets are now available and include access to all sessions, keynotes, exhibitors, visits, professional programme events and networking opportunities.

Further information about tickets can be found on the booking page. For other queries, please email: [conference2023@forarthistory.org.uk](mailto:conference2023@forarthistory.org.uk)

# 2023 Annual Conference

**12-14 APRIL 2023**  
**University College London**

**Welcome!**

We are delighted to welcome you to our **49 th Annual Conference** taking place in-person over three engaging days at **University College London**.

**#ForArtHistory2023** is an opportunity to keep up to date with new research, hear leading keynotes, broaden networks and exchange ideas. Foregrounding critical debate about art, art history and visual cultures in a supportive and inclusive environment is a key remit of the event ensuring that panels and contributing papers represent diverse approaches to the discipline.

Our Annual Conference is open to all and will appeal to academics, curators, practitioners, PhD students, early career researchers and non-art historians engaged with art history research. Members of the Association get reduced conference rates, and concessionary tickets are also available.

Details on each session can be found below.

Conference tickets are now available and include access to all sessions, keynotes, exhibitors, visits, professional programme events and networking opportunities.

Further information about tickets can be found on the booking page. For other queries, please email: [conference2023@forarthistory.org.uk](mailto:conference2023@forarthistory.org.uk)

# ANNUAL CONFERENCE

The annual event for art history in the UK.

Our Annual Conference brings together international research and critical debate about art, art history and visual cultures. This key annual event is an opportunity to keep up to date with new research, hear leading keynotes, broaden networks and exchange ideas.

The Annual Conference is open to all. It is a key annual event for those presenting new research, and those wanting to listen and learn about new research. Attracting around 500 attendees each year, the conference is popular with academics, curators, practitioners, Phd students, early career researchers and non-art historians engaged with art history research. Members of the Association get reduced conference rates.

# ANNUAL CONFERENCE

The annual event for art history in the UK.

Our Annual Conference brings together international research and critical debate about art, art history and visual cultures. This key annual event is an opportunity to keep up to date with new research, hear leading keynotes, broaden networks and exchange ideas.

The Annual Conference is open to all. It is a key annual event for those presenting new research, and those wanting to listen and learn about new research. Attracting around 500 attendees each year, the conference is popular with academics, curators, practitioners, Phd students, early career researchers and non-art historians engaged with art history research. Members of the Association get reduced conference rates.

# 2023 Annual Conference

**12-14 APRIL 2023**  
**University College London**

**Welcome!**

We are delighted to welcome you to our **49 th Annual Conference** taking place in-person over three engaging days at **University College London**.

**#ForArtHistory2023** is an opportunity to keep up to date with new research, hear leading keynotes, broaden networks and exchange ideas. Foregrounding critical debate about art, art history and visual cultures in a supportive and inclusive environment is a key remit of the event ensuring that panels and contributing papers represent diverse approaches to the discipline.

Our Annual Conference is open to all and will appeal to academics, curators, practitioners, PhD students, early career researchers and non-art historians engaged with art history research. Members of the Association get reduced conference rates, and concessionary tickets are also available.

Details on each session can be found below.

Conference tickets are now available and include access to all sessions, keynotes, exhibitors, visits, professional programme events and networking opportunities.

Further information about tickets can be found on the booking page. For other queries, please email: [conference2023@forarthistory.org.uk](mailto:conference2023@forarthistory.org.uk)

[**BOOK NOW!**](https://www.eventbrite.co.uk/e/association-for-art-history-annual-conference-2023-tickets-445107627897)

# 2023 Annual Conference

**12-14 APRIL 2023**  
**University College London**

**Welcome!**

We are delighted to welcome you to our **49 th Annual Conference** taking place in-person over three engaging days at **University College London**.

**#ForArtHistory2023** is an opportunity to keep up to date with new research, hear leading keynotes, broaden networks and exchange ideas. Foregrounding critical debate about art, art history and visual cultures in a supportive and inclusive environment is a key remit of the event ensuring that panels and contributing papers represent diverse approaches to the discipline.

Our Annual Conference is open to all and will appeal to academics, curators, practitioners, PhD students, early career researchers and non-art historians engaged with art history research. Members of the Association get reduced conference rates, and concessionary tickets are also available.

Details on each session can be found below.

Conference tickets are now available and include access to all sessions, keynotes, exhibitors, visits, professional programme events and networking opportunities.

Further information about tickets can be found on the booking page. For other queries, please email: [conference2023@forarthistory.org.uk](mailto:conference2023@forarthistory.org.uk)

[**BOOK NOW!**](https://www.eventbrite.co.uk/e/association-for-art-history-annual-conference-2023-tickets-445107627897)
